meta.description: Geomagnetic storm forecasts made by AI every hour, using open data from satellites and observatories.

footer.disclaimer: Experimental forecasts, made for learning and following along. For serious decisions, check NOAA SWPC.

home.tagline: An artificial intelligence that keeps an eye on the Sun and tells you when a space storm is coming.
home.now_loading: Asking the AI how space is doing…
home.what_p1: We watch the Sun and the space around Earth. We gather data from satellites, probes and observatories all over the world, and an AI uses all of it to forecast geomagnetic storms.
home.what_p2: They are what lights up the auroras, messes with GPS and can trouble satellites and power grids.
home.what_stage1: The Sun throws out gusts of particles and magnetic field…
home.what_stage2: …that reach Earth in hours or days. We try to give a heads-up first.
home.how_1: Every hour, we fetch data from 12 open sources (NOAA, NASA, GFZ, Kyoto and SIDC).
home.how_2: An AI trained on 30 years of history looks at the solar wind, the Sun's explosions and the "mood" of Earth's magnetic field.
home.how_3: It forecasts the Kp and Dst indices for the next 24 hours, along with the chance of a storm.
home.how_4: Every day we compare it with the official NOAA forecast to see who got closer.
home.how_note: Everything is open: the data, the code and the API.

sobre.title: About the forecasts
sobre.subtitle: Everything the AI looks at, how it decides and how we check whether it got it right.
sobre.kp_p1: A score from 0 to 9 that tells how much Earth's magnetic field is "shaking". It comes out every 3 hours, measured by magnetometers spread around the planet.
sobre.kp_p2: Kp 5 or more is a storm (G1). Kp 9 is an extreme storm (G5), like in May 2024.
sobre.dst_p1: Every hour, it measures the strength of a "ring" of electric current that forms around Earth during storms. The more negative, the stronger.
sobre.dst_p2: Below −50 nT it is already a storm. It best shows the effect in places near the equator, like Brazil.
sobre.cme_p1: A coronal mass ejection: a giant bubble of gas and magnetic field that the Sun hurls into space. When it heads toward Earth, it arrives in 1 to 4 days.
sobre.ai_p1: It studied 30 years of solar wind measurements and Earth's indices, looking for the patterns that come before each storm. It doesn't "make things up": it only uses data that exists at the time of the forecast.
sobre.ai_p2: It is retrained every month, but only goes live if it doesn't get worse.
sobre.story_lead: A 150-million-kilometer trip, from the Sun to Earth's sky, in six steps.
sobre.s1_p1: The Sun is a giant ball of electrified gas that spins and churns nonstop. That twists its magnetic field like a wound-up rubber band. Where it gets really twisted, sunspots appear: the active regions.
sobre.s1_ai: NOAA's active regions and the ~11-year cycle (sunspots in OMNI)
sobre.s2_p1: When the twisted field breaks and reconnects, it releases all its stored energy at once: a solar flare. The light and X-rays reach Earth in 8 minutes and can silence radio on the side of the planet facing the Sun.
sobre.s2_ai: the X-ray flux and the flares measured by the GOES satellites
sobre.s3_p1: Sometimes the explosion also hurls a bubble of gas and magnetic field the size of several planets: the CME. It travels at 300 to 3,000 km per second and, if it comes our way, arrives in less than a day up to 4 days.
sobre.s3_p2: Other, weaker storms come from "holes" in the Sun's atmosphere that blow a faster solar wind. Since the Sun turns every ~27 days, they tend to come back on the next turn.
sobre.s3_ai: the CMEs from the CACTus catalog and the 27-day recurrence
sobre.s4_p1: 1.5 million km from Earth, at a spot called L1, there are probes that measure the solar wind before it gets here. When the bubble passes them, we get 15 to 60 minutes of warning.
sobre.s4_ai: the speed, density and magnetic field measured at L1, minute by minute
sobre.s5_p1: Earth is a giant magnet too, and it usually protects us. The secret is the direction of the bubble's magnetic field. If it points south (the famous negative Bz), the two fields click together like magnets with opposite poles, and the Sun's energy gets in. If it points north, almost nothing happens.
sobre.s5_ai: Bz and the Newell coupling function, the most important variables in the model
sobre.s6_p1: The energy that got in makes Earth's magnetic field shake (Kp goes up) and fills a ring of electric current around the planet (Dst goes negative). Particles rain down over the poles and light up the auroras.
sobre.s6_p2: Down here, the storm can make GPS inaccurate, disturb radio, stress satellites and induce currents in power grids. In Brazil, near the equator, the most common effect is on GPS, and the South Atlantic Magnetic Anomaly leaves satellites passing over it more exposed.
sobre.s6_ai: this is what it forecasts: Kp and Dst for the next 24 hours
sobre.travel_title: How long does each thing take to arrive?
sobre.travel_light_text: 8 minutes. They arrive together with the news: no way to warn ahead.
sobre.travel_particles_text: From 20 minutes to a few hours, in radiation storms.
sobre.travel_cme_text: From less than 1 day to 4 days. This is where forecasting makes a difference.
sobre.travel_l1_text: 15 to 60 minutes before the bubble hits Earth.
sobre.formulas_hint: For those who want to see the math behind it. Click each part to open it.
sobre.f_physics: Physical variables computed from the solar wind
sobre.f_clock_text: Interplanetary field components in the GSM system, in nT.
sobre.f_newell_text: Estimates how much solar wind energy gets into the magnetosphere (Newell et al., 2007). v in km/s.
sobre.f_vbs_text: Only counts when Bz points south, the condition that opens up the magnetosphere.
sobre.f_pressure_text: Same formula as the OMNI dataset. n in cm⁻³, v in km/s.
sobre.f_cme_text: For CMEs at least 90° wide. A CME only becomes known to the model at t0 + 6 h, the typical delay of the real-time catalog.
sobre.f_rec_text: Speed, Kp and Dst from one solar rotation ago: fast solar wind streams tend to come back.
sobre.f_gb_text: A sum of M decision trees (up to 1000), each with up to 31 leaves, trained to fix the errors of the previous ones. Learning rate η = 0.05. There is no closed physical formula: the trees learn the relationships from the data.
sobre.f_prob_text: Each model's threshold p* is the one that maximizes HSS in the validation period (2015–2018).
sobre.f_detect_text: A = hits, P = missed storms, F = false alarms, C = correctly forecast calm periods.
sobre.f_hss_text: How much better than chance. It penalizes false alarms, so it is used to choose the alert threshold.
sobre.f_bss_text: o = 1 if there was a storm. The reference is always forecasting the historical frequency.
sobre.f_block_text: Same rule for both sources: nobody is judged with information they didn't have.
sobre.f_winner_title: Who got closer on the day
sobre.f_winner_text: Computed only over blocks where both forecasts and the observed Kp exist. A tie if the difference is under 0.05, and no winner if fewer than half of the blocks are comparable. The observed Kp is GFZ Potsdam's when available, otherwise NOAA's estimate.
sobre.horizon_title: How far ahead does the AI forecast?
sobre.horizon_p1: Every hour, the AI looks at the latest data and makes forecasts for fixed points in the future:
sobre.horizon_kp: Kp: 3, 6, 12 and 24 hours ahead (the 3-hour block that contains each of those moments)
sobre.horizon_p2: The blocks in between are covered by forecasts made in earlier hours: the block 18 h from now, for example, was the "+24 h" of a forecast made 6 hours ago. On the dashboard, each block shows the last forecast made before it started, whatever horizon it came from.
sobre.horizon_p3: That's why a block can show no AI forecast when no earlier forecast reached it yet, for example right after the AI went live or if a data run failed. With the AI running every hour, all blocks in the next 24 hours end up covered.
